stem: Which quotation from The Glass at Ferrow Head most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In Margaret Ilsley's 1894 novel The Glass at Ferrow Head, Hester Quayle keeps the weather records at her father's lighthouse on a stormy northern coast. The village fishermen forecast by signs, such as the color of the dawn or the behavior of gulls, while Hester's notebooks are filled with barometer readings. One critic argues that Ilsley presents Hester as relying on her instrument rather than on local lore even when its readings contradict what the sky itself appears to show: ______
choices: "The sky over the harbor was cloudless, and old Tobin swore by his knee that no blow was coming; but the glass had dropped since noon, and Hester went down to keep the boats in."
"Hester had learned to read the barometer before she could read her primer, and she put more faith in its needle than in any saying the fishermen had about gulls or red mornings."
"Black clouds were piling over Ferrow Head, yet the glass held perfectly steady, and Hester stood at the window a long while, unable to say whether she believed the needle or her eyes."
"The fishermen laughed at the brass barometer in the keeper's window, calling it the lady's clock and declaring that no needle ever made had smelled a storm before a gull did."
explanation: The claim has three parts that must all hold: Hester (1) acts on the barometer (2) instead of local lore, (3) even when the barometer conflicts with what the sky shows. Put choice A in plain words: the sky is clear and a fisherman's sore knee says no storm is coming, but the barometer is falling, so Hester tells the boats to stay in. The clear sky conflicts with the falling barometer, Tobin's knee stands for the lore, and Hester acts on the instrument. All three parts are there.

B.why: You matched the first half of the claim. Hester does trust the needle over the fishermen's sayings, but nothing in this line puts the barometer in conflict with what the sky looks like. You took the 'instrument over lore' part as the whole claim and dropped 'even when it contradicts the sky.'

C.why: You spotted the conflict between the sky and the barometer, which is the hard part of the claim, and stopped there. But in this line Hester can't decide which to believe. That works against a claim that she relies on her instrument. Finding the conflict isn't enough; she also has to act on the barometer.

D.why: This line comes from the right scene, with the barometer up against fishermen's lore, but it describes the fishermen's scorn, not anything Hester believes or does. The claim is about Hester, and she doesn't appear in this line.

stem: Which quotation from The Furrow Year most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Walter Brisco's 1923 novel The Furrow Year follows Ada Lunn, who takes over her late father's wheat farm and, on the advice of a county agent, begins planting clover in alternate years. Clover adds nitrogen to the soil, and the wheat sown in that field the following year draws on the stored nitrogen. A reviewer observed that over the course of the novel, Ada comes to value clover not for its own sake but for what it does for the wheat that follows it: ______
choices: "Ada, who had once thought clover a waste of good ground, came to love that acre for its purple heads and humming bees, though she knew it would never fill a single sack."
"Her father had called a clover field a field on holiday, and for years Ada had agreed with him, begrudging every acre she was obliged to leave out of wheat."
"The acre she had once grudged to clover now gave her the heaviest wheat on the farm, and Ada began to speak of the clover as if it were the first half of the wheat crop."
"The wheat on the east field came up thick and dark that June, taller than any Ada had ever grown, and the neighbors slowed their wagons at the fence to stare at it."
explanation: Break the claim into parts: Ada's view of clover (1) changes ('comes to value'), (2) she values it because of what it does for the next wheat crop, and (3) she does not value it for itself. In plain words, choice C says that the field Ada once resented losing to clover now grows her best wheat, and she starts treating the clover as part of the wheat crop. 'Once grudged' shows the change. Treating clover as 'the first half of the wheat crop' shows she values it only for what it does for the wheat. All three parts are there.

A.why: You saw that the claim describes a change of mind, and this line does show one. But Ada comes to love the clover for its flowers and bees, which is valuing it 'for its own sake,' the very reason the claim rules out. It even says the clover will never 'fill a sack,' so no crop benefit is involved. The tone fits; the reason is the opposite of the claim's.

B.why: This line shows only Ada's earlier view, when she resented clover as lost wheat ground. It is the starting point the claim describes moving away from. Nothing here shows her coming to value clover at all.

D.why: You brought the passage's nitrogen chain into the line. The wheat is impressive, but the quotation never mentions clover or what Ada thinks of it. It's the clover-to-wheat link and Ada's changed view that the claim needs, and you had to add both yourself.

stem: Which quotation from The Fern Ledger most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In Hester Calloway's 1911 novel The Fern Ledger, Agnes Ware spends her summers splitting shale along a Welsh riverbank, looking for fossil plants. Most of what she finds is fragmentary: the tip of a frond, half a stem, a leaf with no plant to belong to. Critic Lionel Dray argues that Agnes recognizes how incomplete her collection is but treats its gaps as a reason to keep searching rather than as a cause for regret: ______
choices: "Every slab I split is a page torn from a book whose other pages the river carried off long before I was born."
"What the shale withholds from me I have simply not earned yet, so tomorrow I try the upper bank."
"I rose before the lark and worked the quarry face until my hands and sleeves were grey with dust."
"The professor says my ferns are common ones, but I would not trade them for all the orchids at Kew."
explanation: Break Dray's claim into its parts: Agnes (1) sees that her collection is incomplete, (2) responds by searching more, and (3) does not respond with regret. In B she names what the shale "withholds," which is the gap. She calls it something she has "not earned yet," so she isn't mourning it, and "tomorrow I try the upper bank" is the further search. All three parts are there.

A.why: You saw incompleteness, the first idea in the claim, and stopped. The torn page and the lost pages do show the gaps, but the tone is loss, which is the regret Dray says Agnes avoids, and nothing in the line has her searching again. This is the half-the-claim trap.

C.why: You matched hard work to "keep searching." The line shows effort, but it says nothing about gaps in the collection, and without the gaps there is nothing for her effort to be a response to.

D.why: You picked the line that shows how attached Agnes is to her fossils. Valuing ordinary specimens is a separate point from seeing the collection's gaps and digging further because of them.

stem: Which quotation from The Tuning Fork most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Oriel Mabry's 1928 play The Tuning Fork follows Bertram Hale, a collector who travels through mining villages writing down folk songs in standard musical notation. Hale is no naive enthusiast. As one theater historian notes, he believes that putting a song on paper changes it, yet he keeps transcribing because he judges an altered song to be better than one that disappears unrecorded: ______
choices: "Put it on the staff and you've pinned a moth to a card. It's still a moth, but it will never fly again."
"Old Maddock sings it different every Sunday, and every Sunday, mind you, it's exactly the right way."
"I know my notation flattens her singing, but a flattened song outlives a song that nobody kept."
"When these singers are gone, their songs go with them, and no one in the city will even notice."
explanation: The claim has three parts: (1) writing a song down changes it, (2) Hale keeps doing it anyway, and (3) his reason is that an altered song is better than a lost one. In C, "my notation flattens her singing" is the change, and "a flattened song outlives a song that nobody kept" weighs the altered version against loss and prefers it. The present-tense "I know... but" shows him carrying on.

A.why: The pinned moth is a strong picture of notation changing a song, so it matches the first part. It gives no reason for continuing, and taken alone it sounds like a case against transcribing. This is the half-the-claim trap.

B.why: The line is about how a song varies from one performance to the next, which is the same general topic. It doesn't say that writing the song down changes it, and it gives no reason to keep transcribing.

D.why: You found the fear of loss, which is Hale's motive, and stopped there. The line never admits that notation changes a song, so the trade-off at the center of the claim is missing.

stem: Which quotation from Notes from the Water Ward most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In Notes from the Water Ward (1874), physician Edwin Strachan recounts tracing a cholera outbreak in a crowded district of Leeds to a single contaminated pump. The book is unusual among medical memoirs of its period. Strachan credits a resident, rather than his own training, with first identifying the source, and he admits that he had initially dismissed what she told him: ______
choices: "In March a laundress told me the pump water smelled of the drain; I noted her down as a gossip, and she was right."
"Kell Street knew its own water better than any physician did, and in time I learned to ask before I sampled it."
"Once the pump handle was taken off, the cases fell away within the week, just as my own figures had predicted."
"The families there received me kindly, though they had little reason to trust a stranger in a frock coat."
explanation: Three things have to hold: (1) a resident identified the source, (2) Strachan gives her the credit, and (3) he had first dismissed her. In A, the laundress connects the pump to the drain, which is the source. "I noted her down as a gossip" is the dismissal, and "she was right" gives her the credit. No other choice includes the dismissal.

B.why: This line does credit the residents over physicians, which is the claim's main attitude, so it survives a first check. It speaks about the street in general, though. No resident identifies the pump, and "in time I learned" isn't the same as admitting he dismissed something specific he was told. You read more into it than it says.

C.why: This is the right scene, since the pump is the source, but the credit goes to the wrong person. "Just as my own figures had predicted" credits Strachan's own calculations, the opposite of what the claim says.

D.why: The line is about how the residents treated Strachan, not about who found the source of the outbreak. It's on topic but has nothing to do with the claim.

stem: Which quotation from "Warp and Weft" most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Clara Densmore's 1902 poem "Warp and Weft" is spoken by a woman who works a loom in a Lancashire cotton mill. Many mill poems of the era protest the anonymity of factory labor. Densmore's speaker, one critic observes, also recognizes that the cloth she makes will reach strangers who will never know who made it, but she finds that anonymity consoling rather than bitter: ______
choices: "The shuttle's click is all my song from lamplight unto lamp; / my fingers know the threads by heart, though cold and stiff and damp."
"Some merchant sells the bolt I wove and pockets what I'm owed; / my name goes nowhere with the cloth along the river road."
"I pray the cloth will keep her warm, whoever she may be, / and wonder if by firelight she ever thinks of me."
"Some woman in a distant town will wear my Tuesday on her sleeve; / she'll never learn who made it, and I find I do not grieve."
explanation: The claim needs (1) cloth reaching strangers, (2) the maker staying unknown, and (3) the speaker being at peace with that. In D, the "woman in a distant town" is the stranger, "she'll never learn who made it" is the anonymity, and "I find I do not grieve" is the consolation. Only this line has all three.

A.why: The line shows the speaker's labor and skill, but nothing travels to a stranger and the question of being known never comes up. It gets the setting right and says nothing about the claim.

B.why: Here the cloth does travel and her name doesn't go with it, so the anonymity is there. The feeling is resentment over pay withheld, which is the bitterness the claim says she avoids. This is the half-the-claim trap: the right situation with the opposite attitude.

C.why: The warm tone and the unknown wearer make this look right. But wondering whether the wearer "ever thinks of me" shows a wish to be known, so she hasn't accepted the anonymity. You caught the tone and missed the attitude.

stem: Which quotation from The Marsh Census most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Darnell Okafor's 1957 novel The Marsh Census centers on Ruth Pell, a warden who counts birds on a coastal reserve that a county council plans partly to drain. The council's surveyors note that herons do not nest in the eastern marsh and conclude that draining it is safe. Ruth, the narrator makes clear, understands that the drainage will harm the herons, but only indirectly, by first eliminating the frogs they feed on: ______
choices: "Drain the east pools and the frogs go first; the herons will follow them out by the second spring."
"The herons don't nest in the east marsh at all. They fish it, and that's a different thing entirely."
"Every April the frogs in the east pools start up so loud I can't hear the herons out on the river."
"If they drain the east marsh, they'll lose the herons that very summer, and you may mark my words."
explanation: The claim is a chain: drainage removes frogs, and losing the frogs harms the herons. It is also indirect and delayed. A gives both steps in order ("the frogs go first") and puts the herons' loss later ("by the second spring"), so it shows the middle link and the delay.

B.why: Ruth does push back on the surveyors here, so a student who sees that she disagrees with them stops at this line. But she never says drainage will harm the herons and never mentions frogs. You supplied the chain yourself; the line doesn't show it.

C.why: Frogs and herons appear together, but the line is about noise. It describes no drainage, no feeding link and no harm.

D.why: This line predicts harm, but harm that is direct and immediate ("that very summer") with no frogs in between. The claim specifically says the harm is indirect.

stem: Which quotation from "The Second Trench" most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In Imelda Rusk's 1966 short story "The Second Trench," archaeologist Nathaniel Abara directs a dig whose sponsors expect treasure. Abara's own interests lie elsewhere. One reviewer argues that Abara values the plain evidence of ordinary life above spectacular finds, while recognizing that it is the spectacular finds that keep his excavation funded: ______
choices: "The museum men want a gold cup for their cases, and they'll pay for next season only if we hand them one."
"Give me a midden full of fish bones over a king's tomb any day, but it's the tomb that pays for the shovels."
"A broken cooking pot will tell you more about how these people lived than any crown ever could."
"We found the gold cup on a Tuesday, and by Friday every newspaper in the capital had sent a man."
explanation: The claim has two parts: (1) Abara prefers ordinary evidence to spectacular finds, and (2) he knows the spectacular finds pay for the dig. In B, "a midden full of fish bones over a king's tomb" is the preference, and "it's the tomb that pays for the shovels" is the funding. Only B has both.

A.why: You found the funding half: sponsors pay only for treasure. The line never shows Abara preferring ordinary evidence, so his own values are missing.

C.why: This line states the preference clearly, and it has the reflective tone you'd expect from Abara, so it's the half-the-claim trap. It says nothing about money, and the claim depends on the tension between what he values and what pays.

D.why: Newspaper attention is connected to spectacular finds, but it isn't funding, and Abara's own preference never appears. This is a detail from the right scene that doesn't support the claim.

stem: Which quotation from The Span most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: Ambrose Feld's 1934 novel The Span follows Clara Voss, a young engineer overseeing a steel bridge across a tidal river. Her superiors urge her to rely on the load tables published by the national Ministry of Works. Voss's habit of mind, as the novel presents it, is precise: she will not accept a load figure simply because an authority has published it, but she will accept one once her own tests have produced it more than once: ______
choices: "The Ministry's tables say the girder will hold, and the Ministry has been wrong before, so we test it."
"I loaded the girder three times and got the same sag each time; that is a number I can build on."
"The Ministry says it will hold. I'll say so too, once my third loading agrees with my first two."
"My father built bridges by feel and memory, and not one of them has fallen in forty years."
explanation: The claim has two parts: (1) a published figure isn't enough for Voss by itself, and (2) she accepts a figure after her own tests have produced it more than once. In C, the Ministry's word isn't enough on its own ("I'll say so too, once..."), and what she requires is repeated agreement ("my third loading agrees with my first two"). Both parts are there.

A.why: This line refuses to take the Ministry on trust and calls for testing, so it holds up after your first good observation. It never says how many tests, though, and the claim depends on "more than once." Taking "we test it" as repeated testing reads in something the line doesn't contain.

B.why: You have the repeated-test half: three loadings, the same result, and a number she accepts. No authority appears, so the line can't show her refusing to accept a published figure.

D.why: Building by feel and memory goes against Voss's reliance on measurement. The line also comes from her father, not her, so it shows nothing about her habit of mind.

stem: Which quotation from The Diet Kitchen most effectively illustrates the claim?
stimulus: In The Diet Kitchen (1923), dietitian Marguerite Lowell draws on two decades of running a children's convalescent home. The book was written partly to correct the nutrition pamphlets of the day, which relied on explaining to children why certain foods were healthful. Lowell holds that children come to eat a food by watching adults enjoy it, not by hearing that it is good for them: ______
choices: "Tell a child that spinach builds the blood and he will believe every word of it, and leave it on his plate."
"A child will copy the adult who feeds him in nearly everything, from how he holds a fork to when he sleeps."
"Children who were allowed to choose their own vegetables at market ate more of them at supper that night."
"One boy ate turnips for a month because I ate them in front of him, plainly and with relish, and said nothing."
explanation: The claim has two parts: (1) children take up a food by watching an adult enjoy it, and (2) not through being told it is healthful. In D, the boy eats turnips "because I ate them in front of him," which is the watching. "With relish" is the enjoyment, and "said nothing" rules out telling. All of it is shown in one line.

A.why: This line shows that telling fails, which is the second half of the claim, and its wry tone sounds like Lowell. It never shows what does work: no adult eats anything, and no child takes up a food. This is the half-the-claim trap.

B.why: This is imitation in general, applied to forks and bedtimes. The claim is narrower: watching an adult enjoy a particular food. A broad statement about copying doesn't show that narrower point, and it leaves out the contrast with telling.

C.why: This credits choosing for oneself, which is a different explanation for why children eat a food. No adult is shown eating anything, so the line doesn't support Lowell's claim.
